AIM:  To create Video Streaming Platform (YouTube-like)

Functional Requirement:. 

  • User registration / login

  • Upload videos

  • Watch videos

  • Like / dislike videos

  • Comment on videos

  • Subscribe to channels

  • View recommended videos

  • Search videos

  • Video history tracking

Non Functional requirements

1. Scalable: 2B users, 100M DAU, Millions of videos uploaded daily

2.Availability vs consistency: Availability > consistency

3. Latency: Video start time < 2 second, API response < 200 ms

MAJOR ENTITIES
A. USER: user_id, username, email, password, channel_name, subscribers_count, created_at
B. Videos: video_id, user_id, title, description, video_url, thumbnail_url, duration, view_count, like_count, upload_time
C. Comments: comment_id, video_id, user_id, text, timestamp
D. Likes: like_id, video_id, user_id, reaction_type
E. Subscription: subscription_id, subscriber_id, channel_id,timestamp

Core API ENDPOINTS:
1. USER:
POST /api/users/register
POST /api/users/login
GET /api/users/{user_id}

2. Videos
POST /api/videos/upload
GET /api/videos/{video_id}
DELETE /api/videos/{video_id}

3. Interaction
POST /api/videos/{video_id}/like
POST /api/videos/{video_id}/comment
POST /api/channels/{channel_id}/subscribe

4. Feed
GET /api/videos/recommendations
GET /api/videos/trending 

5. Search
GET /search?q=keyword – search videos.

Issue: In the current diagram the Upload Service sends videos directly to the Video DB. Databases like MySQL or traditional databases are not designed to store very large binary files such as videos. A single video may be hundreds of megabytes and millions of videos may be uploaded daily. Storing such large files inside the database causes extremely high storage costs, slow queries, database bloating, backup difficulties, and poor performance. The database should ideally store structured metadata, not heavy media files.


Solution: Instead of storing videos inside the database, the system should store video files in an object storage system such as Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, or any distributed object storage. The Video DB will only store metadata like video_id, title, description, duration, video_url, thumbnail_url, and uploader_id. The Upload Service will upload the actual video file to object storage and then store the storage URL in the Video DB. This keeps the database lightweight and improves scalability.

Issue: In the current architecture the Upload Service directly uploads the video to Blob Object Storage and then stores metadata in the Video Metadata database. However, large video platforms cannot store raw uploaded videos directly because they must first process them. Videos need to be encoded into multiple resolutions such as 1080p, 720p, 480p, and 360p so that users with different internet speeds can stream them smoothly. Thumbnails also need to be generated and content moderation may be required. If the Upload Service performs all this processing synchronously, the service becomes very slow and overloaded because video processing is computationally heavy and may take several seconds or minutes.


Solution: Introduce an asynchronous video processing pipeline using a message queue and worker services. Instead of processing the video immediately, the Upload Service will upload the raw video to Blob Storage and then send a message to a message queue containing the video ID and storage location. Worker services will consume tasks from the queue and perform encoding, thumbnail generation, and moderation. After processing, the processed video versions are stored back in object storage and the metadata database is updated with available resolutions and thumbnail URLs. This keeps the Upload Service lightweight and allows the system to scale horizontally by adding more workers.

Issue: In the current architecture the View Service appears to directly serve video content from Blob Object Storage to users. If a video becomes popular and millions of users try to watch it simultaneously, every request will go through the backend services and storage layer. This creates extremely high network bandwidth consumption and request load on the origin infrastructure. Blob storage and backend services are not designed to handle millions of direct streaming requests per second. As traffic grows, the system will experience high latency, increased costs, and possible service outages.


Solution: Introduce a Content Delivery Network (CDN) between users and the video storage. A CDN is a distributed network of edge servers placed across different geographic regions. When users request a video, the CDN serves the cached copy from the nearest edge location instead of always fetching it from the origin storage. Only the first request or cache miss reaches the origin Blob Object Storage. This drastically reduces load on backend services, improves video startup time, and allows the system to scale to millions of concurrent viewers.

Issue: In the current architecture the Video Streaming Service directly queries the Video Metadata database for every request. When millions of users request video information simultaneously, the database must handle extremely high read traffic. Databases are not designed to serve such large volumes of repeated read requests, especially for popular videos. This can lead to increased latency, overloaded database nodes, and reduced system scalability.


Solution: Introduce an in-memory caching layer such as Redis between the Video Streaming Service and the Video Metadata database. Frequently accessed metadata such as video title, duration, CDN URL, thumbnail URLs, and popularity metrics can be stored in Redis. The Video Streaming Service will first check Redis for the requested metadata. If the data exists (cache hit), it returns immediately without querying the database. If the data is missing (cache miss), the service fetches the metadata from the Video Metadata database, returns the result, and stores it in Redis for future requests. This reduces database load and significantly improves response time.
